f: Mozart made up his first little pieces at the age of five, and his dad wrote them down in his big sister’s music book.
At six, Mozart played for Empress Maria Theresa. His dad wrote that the little boy then jumped onto her lap and kissed her!
Little Mozart could play even when the keys were covered with a cloth. Audiences gasped in amazement!
When Wolfgang was seven, the whole family set off on a tour of Europe. It lasted almost three and a half years — in carriages on bumpy roads!
Mozart wrote his first symphony at eight, in London, during days when the house had to be kept quiet and nobody could play the harpsichord.
At fourteen, in Rome, Mozart heard a famous church piece whose music was kept secret — and he wrote it all down from memory!
Mozart bought a starling that whistled a tune from one of his concertos, with just one note sung its own way. Mozart wrote: “That was lovely!”
He wrote twelve variations on an old French song. Children all over the world know its tune: it’s the one we sing to “Twinkle, Twinkle, Little Star”.
Mozart wrote out one of his horn concertos in four colours of ink — red, green, blue and black — to make his horn-playing friend laugh.
Mozart wrote music for the glass harmonica: its glass bowls sing when you touch them with wet fingers. The instrument was invented by Benjamin Franklin.
His opera The Magic Flute has a cheerful bird-catcher called Papageno, dressed in feathers. He has a little pipe and a set of magic bells.
Mozart loved playing billiards and had his very own billiard table at home.

tf.s: Mozart’s big sister, Nannerl, was a young star too and performed with him.
tf.w: Brother and sister played together for kings, queens and audiences all over Europe.

tf.s: Mozart wrote the tune of “Twinkle, Twinkle, Little Star”.
tf.w: It’s an old French song that existed before Mozart. He wrote twelve variations on its tune.

tf.s: The name Amadeus means “king of music”.
tf.w: The name is made from the Latin words for “love” and “God”.

tf.s: Mozart wrote more than six hundred pieces of music.
tf.w: A scholar called Ludwig Köchel made a list of them, and it has more than six hundred numbers.

tf.s: Mozart spent his whole life in his home town of Salzburg and never travelled.
tf.w: He visited London, Paris, Rome and Prague, and as a grown-up he lived in Vienna.

tf.s: Mozart’s music is travelling through space.
tf.w: In 1977 the Voyager spacecraft set off carrying a golden record of music from Earth, and it includes an aria from The Magic Flute.

f: When Tchaikovsky was little, his family had an orchestrion — a music machine that played by itself. Little Pyotr listened to Mozart’s music on it.
At first Tchaikovsky worked at the Ministry of Justice, and he only started studying music seriously at twenty-one.
For The Nutcracker he found the celesta in Paris — it tinkles like magic bells. He wanted it kept secret so nobody else used it first.
Tchaikovsky dedicated his Children’s Album to his nephew Volodya. It has pieces about a doll, wooden soldiers and playing horses.
The Nutcracker is based on a fairy tale by the German writer Hoffmann: on Christmas night the toys come alive and the Nutcracker becomes a prince.
In the ballet The Sleeping Beauty, fairy-tale guests come to the wedding: Puss in Boots with the White Cat, and Little Red Riding Hood with the Wolf.
In Swan Lake, Princess Odette is a white swan by day and only becomes a girl again at night.
He wrote The Seasons — twelve piano pieces, one for each month. A magazine printed one every month for a whole year.
In 1891 Tchaikovsky sailed to America and conducted at the opening of the famous Carnegie Hall in New York.
He loved long walks in the woods and enjoyed picking mushrooms and flowers.
Tchaikovsky and Nadezhda von Meck, who helped him with money, wrote each other more than 1,200 letters — but they agreed never to meet!
The music of the 1812 Overture includes cannon shots and ringing bells. At outdoor concerts, real cannons sometimes go BOOM — without cannonballs, of course!

tf.s: Real swans dance in Swan Lake.
tf.w: The swans are danced by ballerinas in white, puffy skirts called tutus.

tf.s: Tchaikovsky was born in Votkinsk, where his dad ran a big ironworks.
tf.w: His father managed the Votkinsk works, and little Pyotr spent his first years there.

tf.s: The celesta sounds loud, like a big drum.
tf.w: The celesta looks like a small piano and tinkles softly, like little bells.

tf.s: The University of Cambridge in England made Tchaikovsky an honorary Doctor of Music.
tf.w: He received the honour in 1893 and wore a grand ceremonial gown.

tf.s: Tchaikovsky was friends with the Norwegian composer Grieg.
tf.w: They met in Leipzig in 1888, and Tchaikovsky dedicated his Hamlet overture to Grieg.

tf.s: Tchaikovsky only ever wrote ballets.
tf.w: He also wrote operas, symphonies, concertos, songs and lots of piano pieces.

f: Beethoven gave his first concert at seven. His dad wrote on the poster that he was six, to make the boy seem even more amazing.
As a teenager, Beethoven already had jobs: he played the organ and the viola in the orchestra of his home town, Bonn.
At twenty-one, Beethoven moved to Vienna and took lessons from the great Haydn himself.
In Vienna, Beethoven moved house so often that he lived in dozens of different flats.
He loved walks in the countryside and always carried a notebook to jot down tunes that popped into his head.
In his Sixth Symphony you can hear a babbling brook, a nightingale, a quail and a cuckoo — and then a thunderstorm.
The Fifth Symphony begins with just four notes: da-da-da-DUM! Almost everyone in the world recognises them.
Nobody knows for sure who Elise was in his famous piece Für Elise. It’s still a musical mystery!
When Beethoven’s hearing grew weak, friends wrote their questions in notebooks and he answered out loud. More than a hundred of these “conversation books” survive.
His assistant said Beethoven made his coffee from exactly sixty beans — and counted every one!
At the premiere of his Ninth Symphony, Beethoven couldn’t hear the applause. A singer turned him round — and he saw people clapping and waving their hats.
The tune of the “Ode to Joy” from his Ninth Symphony is played today as the anthem of Europe.

tf.s: Beethoven was born deaf.
tf.w: As a child he heard perfectly well; he began to lose his hearing in his late twenties.

tf.s: Beethoven had special ear trumpets, like little megaphones.
tf.w: They were made by the inventor Mälzel, famous for his metronomes, and you can still see them in a museum in Bonn.

tf.s: Nobody knows Beethoven’s exact birthday.
tf.w: We only know he was baptised on 17 December 1770; he was probably born the day before.

tf.s: Beethoven himself named his “Moonlight” Sonata.
tf.w: A music critic gave it that name many years later, because the music reminded him of moonlight on a lake.

tf.s: Beethoven wrote lots of operas.
tf.w: He wrote only one opera, Fidelio — but he composed four different overtures for it!

tf.s: Beethoven’s music is on a golden record travelling through space.
tf.w: The record on the Voyager spacecraft has the opening of his Fifth Symphony and another of his pieces.

f: Bach had twenty children! Four of his sons became famous composers too.
Bach’s sons told this story: as a boy, he secretly copied music at night, by moonlight, from his big brother’s locked cupboard.
As a teenager, Bach set off for the faraway town of Lüneburg to sing in a boys’ choir — he had a beautiful, clear voice.
At twenty, he walked about 400 kilometres to hear the famous organist Buxtehude — and stayed four months instead of one!
Bach was a great organist. An organ has thousands of pipes, from tiny ones the size of a pencil to huge ones taller than a house.
He was often asked to test new organs. First he pulled out all the stops, joking that he wanted to know if the organ had good lungs.
Bach wrote a funny Coffee Cantata about a girl who loves coffee so much that her father can’t get her to give it up.
In his first years in Leipzig, Bach wrote a new cantata almost every week — one for each Sunday!
In German, the name Bach means “brook” — a little stream. Beethoven supposedly joked that he should have been called not Brook but Sea.
There’s a legend that Bach wrote the Goldberg Variations for a count who couldn’t sleep, and a musician called Goldberg played them to him at night.
One of his tunes was later rearranged so a violinist can play it on just one string. That’s how the “Air on the G String” came about.
Over time, Bach’s music was rarely performed. Almost eighty years after his death, young Mendelssohn put on his St Matthew Passion — and the world loved Bach again.

tf.s: Bach himself wrote the famous Minuet in G from Anna Magdalena’s music notebook.
tf.w: Invented, although people believed it for a very long time! Scholars found out it was written by another composer, Christian Petzold; Bach’s family just copied it into the notebook.

tf.s: Bach’s music is travelling through space.
tf.w: The golden record on the Voyager spacecraft has three of his pieces — more than any other composer.

tf.s: Bach was once kept under arrest for nearly a month because he wanted to change jobs.
tf.w: The Duke of Weimar didn’t want to let him go. In the end he did, and Bach went to work in Köthen.

tf.s: Bach had only one child.
tf.w: He had twenty children, and there was always music in the house.

tf.s: Bach wrote more than a thousand pieces of music.
tf.w: The catalogue of his music has more than a thousand numbers.

tf.s: Bach travelled all over the world giving concerts.
tf.w: Bach spent his whole life in Germany and never once went abroad.

f: Vivaldi was nicknamed “the Red Priest” because of his fiery red hair.
His father was a barber who became a violinist at St Mark’s Basilica in Venice. He taught his son to play the violin.
Vivaldi was born in Venice — a city with canals instead of streets and boats called gondolas instead of cars.
Vivaldi became a priest, but soon stopped saying Mass because he sometimes found it hard to breathe. So he gave his life to music.
He taught music to girls at an orphanage in Venice, and their orchestra was famous all over Europe.
Many of the orphanage girls had no surnames, so they were named after their instruments — for example, Anna Maria of the Violin.
The Four Seasons comes with poems, and the music tells what they describe: birdsong, a thunderstorm, summer heat and winter frost.
In the concerto “Spring”, the viola plays a dog barking beside a sleeping shepherd.
In “Winter” you can hear teeth chattering with cold and people walking carefully on slippery ice.
Vivaldi boasted that he could compose a concerto faster than a copyist could copy it out!
He wrote about five hundred concertos, and almost forty of them are for the bassoon, a low wooden wind instrument.
Vivaldi’s music lay forgotten for a long time. Many of his scores were found only about a hundred years ago — now the whole world knows The Four Seasons.

tf.s: The Four Seasons is a set of songs for a choir.
tf.w: It’s four concertos for violin and orchestra, with no words — but each one has a poem to go with it.

tf.s: Bach arranged several of Vivaldi’s concertos for organ and harpsichord.
tf.w: Bach liked Vivaldi’s music so much that he rewrote it for his own instruments.

tf.s: Vivaldi taught music to boys at a naval school.
tf.w: He taught the girls of a Venice orphanage called the Pietà.

tf.s: Vivaldi wrote operas as well as concertos.
tf.w: He said himself that he had written ninety-four operas, though the music of some is lost.

tf.s: Vivaldi wrote concertos for the mandolin.
tf.w: The mandolin is a small stringed instrument played with a plectrum.

tf.s: Vivaldi was a famous trumpet player.
tf.w: Vivaldi was a famous, dazzling violinist.

f: Grieg was very short — about one and a half metres tall. But the whole world knows his music!
He always carried a little frog figurine in his pocket for good luck.
Edvard’s mum began teaching him the piano when he was six.
As a boy, Grieg once stood under a drainpipe on purpose to get soaked, so he’d be sent home instead of having lessons. Later he told this himself, laughing.
The famous violinist Ole Bull heard fifteen-year-old Edvard play and persuaded his parents to send him to study music in Germany.
Grieg wrote music for the play Peer Gynt at the request of its writer, Henrik Ibsen. It’s about Peer, a cheeky young man who tells tall tales.
“In the Hall of the Mountain King” is music about trolls: it starts very, very quietly, then gets faster and louder.
Grieg named his house near Bergen Troldhaugen — “Troll Hill”.
Near the house, right by the water, stood a tiny hut with a piano, where Grieg composed while looking out at the water.
He wrote sixty-six Lyric Pieces for piano — about a butterfly, a little bird, spring and even a march of trolls.
In 1903 Grieg recorded his own playing on a gramophone, and you can still listen to those recordings today.
Grieg’s great-grandfather came to Norway from Scotland, where the family name was spelt a little differently: Greig.

tf.s: Grieg kept a real, live frog in his pocket.
tf.w: It was a little frog figurine — a lucky charm.

tf.s: Grieg was friends with Tchaikovsky.
tf.w: They met in Leipzig, and Tchaikovsky dedicated his Hamlet overture to Grieg.

tf.s: “Morning” from Peer Gynt shows the sun rising over the mountains of Norway.
tf.w: Invented, although many people think so! In the play it’s morning in Morocco, in Africa, where Peer ends up on his travels.

tf.s: Grieg’s wife Nina was a singer who sang his songs.
tf.w: Nina sang while Edvard played the piano for her. He wrote the song “I Love You” for her.

tf.s: Grieg turned Norwegian folk tunes into his own pieces.
tf.w: He loved the songs and dances of Norwegian village musicians and made piano pieces from them.

tf.s: Grieg was a giant, two metres tall.
tf.w: He was very short — about one and a half metres.

f: Haydn’s dad, a village wheelwright, played the harp in the evenings. Little Joseph held a stick like a bow and “played the violin” along with him.
From the age of eight, Haydn sang in the boys’ choir of the great St Stephen’s Cathedral in Vienna.
It’s said that young Haydn, as a choirboy, once snipped off another choirboy’s pigtail as a joke.
Musicians fondly called him “Papa Haydn” — he was kind and always stood up for them.
For almost thirty years Haydn worked for the Esterházy princes, writing music for their concerts, operas and celebrations.
Once the prince kept his musicians away from home too long. So in Haydn’s “Farewell” Symphony, the players blew out their candles and left one by one.
In the “Surprise” Symphony, quiet music suddenly goes — BANG! — with a loud chord. Haydn himself said he wanted to surprise the audience with something new.
His symphonies have funny nicknames: “The Bear”, “The Hen” and “The Clock”. In “The Clock”, the music ticks like a pendulum.
In his oratorio The Creation, the music shows a roaring lion, a leaping tiger, a galloping horse and even a creeping worm.
Haydn first went to sea when he was nearly sixty, on his way to London. There he was welcomed like a real star.
Haydn wrote more than a hundred symphonies, which is why he is called “the father of the symphony”.
A tune Haydn wrote in honour of the Austrian emperor is sung today as the national anthem of Germany.

tf.s: Haydn was called “Papa” because he had lots of children.
tf.w: Haydn had no children of his own. The musicians called him “Papa” because he looked after them.

tf.s: Haydn and Mozart were friends.
tf.w: Mozart dedicated six string quartets to Haydn, and Haydn said Mozart was the greatest composer he knew.

tf.s: Haydn wrote the Toy Symphony, which uses toy instruments.
tf.w: Invented, although people thought so for a very long time. Scholars found out it was written by another composer.

tf.s: Haydn wrote a trumpet concerto.
tf.w: He wrote it for a new kind of trumpet with keys, which could play many more notes.

tf.s: Haydn gave lessons to the young Beethoven.
tf.w: When young Beethoven came to Vienna, he studied with Haydn for a while.

tf.s: As a child, Haydn was a child star who toured Europe with his family.
tf.w: Haydn grew up in a simple family and sang in a church choir; fame came to him much later.

f: Rossini was born on 29 February, so his real birthday only came round once every four years!
His dad played the trumpet and the horn, and his mum was a singer, so there was music in the house from the very start.
Rossini wrote his first opera when he was still a teenager.
Rossini was nicknamed “Signor Crescendo”: in his music a tune often repeats, getting louder and louder each time.
He composed the opera The Barber of Seville very quickly — in less than three weeks.
It’s said the first night of The Barber went all wrong — a cat even walked onto the stage! Later it became one of the world’s best-loved operas.
In The Barber, cheerful Figaro sings “Figaro here, Figaro there!” — because the whole town needs him.
In Rossini’s opera Cinderella there is no glass slipper: the prince recognises Cinderella by her bracelet.
The gallop from the William Tell Overture is often heard in cartoons when the heroes ride off on horseback.
Rossini wrote his last opera at 37, then lived almost forty more years, composing for himself and his friends.
In old age he wrote playful little pieces and called them “Radishes”, “Anchovies”, “Butter” and “Dried Figs”.
Rossini loved good food, and a beef steak with truffles is still named after him: “tournedos Rossini”.

tf.s: Rossini worked as a chef in a restaurant.
tf.w: He was a composer — he just loved cooking and eating good food.

tf.s: Rossini spent the last years of his life in Paris.
tf.w: He lived in Paris and held musical evenings for his friends at home.

tf.s: The overture to The Barber of Seville was first written for a different opera.
tf.w: Rossini had already used it for two of his earlier operas before he took it for The Barber.

tf.s: The William Tell gallop was written specially for a cartoon.
tf.w: Rossini wrote it for an opera in 1829 — long before films were invented.

tf.s: Rossini was born in Spain, in Seville.
tf.w: He was born in Italy, in the town of Pesaro. Seville is where his opera takes place.

tf.s: In Rossini’s Cinderella there is a funny stepfather instead of a wicked stepmother.
tf.w: A boastful stepfather, Don Magnifico, is unkind to Cinderella, and instead of a fairy godmother she is helped by the prince’s wise tutor.

f: Johann Strauss was called “the Waltz King”, and all of Vienna danced to his waltzes.
His dad was a famous composer too, but he wanted his son to work in a bank. His mum helped the boy take violin lessons in secret.
At eighteen, Strauss formed his own orchestra and gave his first concert — the audience loved it.
Strauss conducted standing in front of the orchestra with a violin in his hands — and played along with everyone.
People have been dancing to his waltz “The Blue Danube” for more than a hundred and fifty years.
“The Blue Danube” was first a song for a men’s choir, and only later became the famous waltz for orchestra.
In a famous film, spaceships glide gracefully through space to “The Blue Danube”.
Every year on 1 January, Vienna holds a New Year’s Concert, and “The Blue Danube” is almost always played.
He wrote the “Pizzicato Polka” with his brother Josef. The musicians play it without bows — they pluck the strings with their fingers.
In his polka “Thunder and Lightning”, drums and cymbals crash like a real storm.
Strauss wrote the operetta Die Fledermaus (“The Bat”) — a funny story with a masked ball and lots of mix-ups.
In 1872 Strauss sailed to America and in Boston conducted a gigantic festival concert with thousands of singers and musicians!

tf.s: Strauss was an only child.
tf.w: He had brothers, Josef and Eduard, and they became musicians too.

tf.s: The Radetzky March, which the whole audience claps along to at the New Year’s Concert, was written by Strauss’s father.
tf.w: It was composed by Johann Strauss the Elder in 1848.

tf.s: Die Fledermaus is an operetta about a real bat.
tf.w: “The Bat” is the nickname of a character who once went to a masked ball dressed as a bat.

tf.s: Strauss wrote more than five hundred waltzes, polkas and other dances.
tf.w: He wrote dance music all his life.

tf.s: Brahms admired “The Blue Danube”.
tf.w: Brahms once wrote its opening bars on the fan of Strauss’s wife and added: “Unfortunately not by Johannes Brahms”.

tf.s: Strauss only wrote slow lullabies.
tf.w: He wrote waltzes and fast, jolly polkas that all of Vienna danced to.

f: At twelve, Nikolai went to the naval college — just like his big brother, who was a sailor.
Rimsky-Korsakov was a naval officer and spent more than two years at sea on a ship, visiting England, America and Brazil.
He was one of the “Mighty Handful” — a close group of five composers who wanted to write Russian music.
For a while he and Mussorgsky shared one room and one piano: Mussorgsky composed at it in the morning, and Rimsky-Korsakov in the afternoon.
Asked to teach at the conservatoire, he still didn’t know a lot himself — so he studied in secret to stay one step ahead of his students.
He wrote fairy-tale operas: The Snow Maiden, Sadko, The Tale of Tsar Saltan and The Golden Cockerel.
“The Flight of the Bumblebee” comes from the opera The Tale of Tsar Saltan: Prince Gvidon turns into a bumblebee to fly to his father.
In the same opera, a squirrel cracks golden nuts and sings a Russian folk song, “In the Garden, in the Vegetable Patch”.
In The Golden Cockerel, the magic cockerel crows: “Cock-a-doodle-doo! Rule on, lying on your side!”
In Scheherazade, the solo violin is Scheherazade herself, telling the sultan the tales of the Thousand and One Nights.
To Rimsky-Korsakov, music had colours: one key seemed white to him, another sunny yellow, another sapphire blue.
His students included Igor Stravinsky and Sergei Prokofiev, who later became great composers themselves.

tf.s: Rimsky and Korsakov were two different composers.
tf.w: It’s one man with a double surname — Nikolai Rimsky-Korsakov.

tf.s: Rimsky-Korsakov wrote a textbook about how to write for an orchestra.
tf.w: Musicians still read his book Principles of Orchestration today.

tf.s: Rimsky-Korsakov helped finish his friend Borodin’s opera Prince Igor.
tf.w: Borodin didn’t manage to complete it, so his friends Rimsky-Korsakov and Glazunov finished the opera.

tf.s: Scheherazade is a heroine of Russian fairy tales.
tf.w: Scheherazade is the storyteller of the Thousand and One Nights, tales from the Middle East.

tf.s: The opera Sadko is about a musician who visits an underwater kingdom.
tf.w: Sadko plays his gusli — an old Russian stringed instrument — so well that the Sea King himself starts to dance.

tf.s: Rimsky-Korsakov wrote only one opera.
tf.w: He wrote fifteen operas, and many of them are based on fairy tales.

f: Little Modest’s nanny told him Russian fairy tales, and he loved them all his life.
At nine, Modest played a big piano concerto by the composer John Field in front of guests.
At seventeen, Mussorgsky became an officer in the Guards, but he soon left the army to devote himself to music.
He wrote Pictures at an Exhibition after an exhibition of drawings by his friend, the artist and architect Viktor Hartmann.
Mussorgsky wrote Pictures very quickly — in about three weeks.
The “Promenade” comes between the pieces: it’s Mussorgsky himself strolling through the exhibition from picture to picture.
The piece “Gnomus” is based on a drawing by Hartmann: a little gnome waddling clumsily on crooked legs.
“Ballet of the Unhatched Chicks” is based on costume designs for a ballet: chicks peeking out of their eggshells.
Baba Yaga’s hut on hen’s legs was, in Hartmann’s drawing… a design for a clock! In Mussorgsky’s music, Baba Yaga dashes off in her flying mortar.
In “Tuileries”, children play and squabble in a Paris park while their nannies try to calm them.
The last piece, “The Great Gate of Kyiv”, comes from a design for a city gate that was never built. The music rings out grandly, like bells.
In his song cycle The Nursery, Mussorgsky wrote the words himself: a boy chats with his nanny, plays with his doll and rides a hobby horse.

tf.s: Mussorgsky painted the pictures for the exhibition himself.
tf.w: The drawings were by his friend Viktor Hartmann; Mussorgsky “painted” them in music.

tf.s: Pictures at an Exhibition was first written for piano alone.
tf.w: The famous version for orchestra was made later by the French composer Maurice Ravel.

tf.s: For a while, Mussorgsky and Rimsky-Korsakov lived in the same room.
tf.w: They shared a room and a piano, and each of them was writing an opera there.

tf.s: The words of The Nursery songs were written by Pushkin.
tf.w: Mussorgsky made up the words of these songs himself.

tf.s: Mussorgsky wrote a funny song about a king who dressed a flea in a velvet coat.
tf.w: It’s the “Song of the Flea”: the king loved his flea so much that he made it a minister.

tf.s: Real chicks danced in the “Ballet of the Unhatched Chicks”.
tf.w: Hartmann drew costumes for performers: chicks in their eggshells.

f: Brahms’s dad played the double bass in Hamburg and was the first to teach his son music.
Johannes started piano lessons at seven, and by ten he was already performing in public.
As a teenager, Brahms gave lessons and played the piano for money to help his family.
His Lullaby is sung to babies all over the world. He wrote it as a present for a friend who had just had a baby boy.
Young Brahms was greatly encouraged by the composer Robert Schumann and his wife Clara, a famous pianist. Brahms stayed friends with Clara all his life.
His Hungarian Dances were first written for two pianists sharing one piano — for four hands.
As a young man Brahms had no beard. He grew the big beard you see in his portraits when he was over forty.
Brahms began his First Symphony as a young man and only finished it at 43: he badly wanted it to be as good as Beethoven’s.
In 1889 Brahms played his music for Edison’s phonograph. It’s one of the very first recordings of a great composer playing.
When a university made him an honorary doctor, Brahms said thank you by writing a cheerful overture full of student songs.
Brahms loved walking, and in summer he went off to compose in beautiful places — in the mountains or by lakes.
Bach, Beethoven and Brahms are known as “the three Bs”.

tf.s: Brahms wrote waltzes too.
tf.w: He wrote sixteen waltzes for piano, and one of them is very famous.

tf.s: Brahms wrote his Lullaby for his own child.
tf.w: Brahms had no children of his own. He wrote it as a present for a friend’s baby.

tf.s: Brahms was a famous double bass player.
tf.w: It was his dad who played the double bass; Brahms himself was a wonderful pianist.

tf.s: Brahms wrote a violin concerto for a violinist friend.
tf.w: He wrote it for the famous violinist Joseph Joachim.

tf.s: Brahms helped the Czech composer Dvořák become famous.
tf.w: Brahms liked young Dvořák’s music and advised his own publisher to print it.

tf.s: Brahms was born in Vienna.
tf.w: He was born in Hamburg, in the north of Germany, and moved to Vienna as a grown-up.
